bodyHtml:
Top ten films about translation and interpreting

July 11, 2019
E-learning | Education | International Development | Training

Cinema is one of the best ways to explore other languages and cultures, and a good number of films put translation and interpreting at the centre of the story. Some follow a linguist trying to decode an alien language, others use an interpreter's booth as the setting for a thriller, and a few show what happens when meaning gets lost between two languages.

Here are ten films about translation, interpreting and subtitling that are worth watching, whether you work with languages or simply enjoy them.

Arrival (Denis Villeneuve, 2016)

Amy Adams plays Louise Banks, a linguist recruited to communicate with extraterrestrial visitors. The film, adapted from Ted Chiang's short story "Story of Your Life", turns the work of decoding an unfamiliar language into a gripping drama.

It also asks what happens to the way you think when you learn a new language. Few films take the craft of linguistic analysis as seriously.

Charade (Stanley Donen, 1963)

Audrey Hepburn plays Regina Lampert, an American simultaneous interpreter living in Paris, who finds herself in a tangled mystery alongside Cary Grant. The interpreting is a backdrop rather than the plot, but the film remains a stylish classic.

It is a good pick if you enjoy a comedy thriller with an international cast.

Lost in Translation (Sofia Coppola, 2003)

Bill Murray plays Bob Harris, an actor in Tokyo to shoot a whisky commercial, and Scarlett Johansson plays Charlotte, a young woman he meets at his hotel. The film is about loneliness and connection, but it is also remembered for a scene in which a director gives long instructions and the interpreter passes on a much shorter version.

Anyone who has worked with interpreters will recognise the moment. It shows why a skilled interpreter conveys intent and tone, not only words.

The Terminal (Steven Spielberg, 2004)

Tom Hanks plays Viktor Navorski, a traveller who lands in New York with almost no English and cannot leave the airport. The film is loosely inspired by Mehran Karimi Nasseri, an Iranian refugee who lived in Paris Charles de Gaulle airport from 1988 to 2006.

Watch how Viktor learns English from the world around him, and how much of the story depends on who is available to translate.

The Interpreter (Sydney Pollack, 2005)

Nicole Kidman plays Silvia Broome, a United Nations interpreter who overhears a conversation that puts her life in danger. The thriller is built around the booth, the headset and the trust placed in interpreters.

If you like this one, Charade and The Covenant also put interpreters in the spotlight.

Spanglish (James L. Brooks, 2004)

This comedy drama follows Flor, a Mexican single mother who works for a wealthy family in California, with Paz Vega, Adam Sandler and Téa Leoni. The cultural and linguistic gaps between the characters drive both the humour and the heartache.

It is a useful reminder that unclear communication has real consequences, at home as much as at work. A professional Spanish translator would have saved the characters some trouble.

Okja (Bong Joon-ho, 2017)

Okja is not a film about translation, but its subtitles contain one of the best-known translation jokes in recent cinema. In one scene the English subtitle tells Mija to try learning English because it opens new doors, while the Korean dialogue is actually a character telling her his name.

Bong Joon-ho has explained that the original line would not work for English-speaking audiences, so he and co-writer Jon Ronson wrote a different joke. That is localisation at its most creative, and a good example of why Korean audiovisual translation needs a linguist who understands both humour and culture.

Welcome to the Sticks (Dany Boon, 2008)

A French post office manager is transferred to the north of France, where locals speak the Ch'ti dialect that he cannot understand. Much of the comedy depends on language, which makes the English subtitles a real challenge.

It is a good film to watch if you want to see how a regional dialect works as a source of humour, and how subtitlers try to carry it into another language.

Chuck Norris vs Communism (Ilinca Călugăreanu, 2015)

This documentary looks at how smuggled Western films reached Romanian audiences in the 1980s. Irina Nistor dubbed many of the banned VHS tapes into Romanian, and her voice became one of the most recognisable in the country, even though most viewers never knew who she was.

The film is a fascinating look at dubbing under censorship, and a reminder of how much power sits with the person who translates. You can read more about the craft in the BeTranslated post on movie dubbing.

The Covenant (Guy Ritchie, 2023)

Jake Gyllenhaal plays a US Army sergeant in Afghanistan and Dar Salim plays Ahmed, the Afghan interpreter who works with his unit. The story turns on the debt the soldier feels towards his interpreter, and reviewers link it to the treatment of Afghan interpreters after the withdrawal.

It is a very different film from the lighter titles on this list, and it shows that interpreters often work in high-risk settings.

Why subtitles and interpreting still matter for film

When Bong Joon-ho accepted the Golden Globe for Best Foreign Language Film for Parasite in January 2020, he spoke about the "one-inch-tall barrier of subtitles". His interpreter, Sharon Choi, was widely praised for her interpreting.

Those two moments sum up the point of this list. Whether on screen or on stage, someone has to carry meaning, tone and humour from one language to another, and that takes training.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best film about translation?

Arrival is often the first choice for its serious treatment of linguistics, while Lost in Translation is the best known for showing the gap between what is said and what is understood. The Interpreter and The Covenant are good choices if you want to see professional interpreters at the centre of the story.

Which films feature a conference interpreter?

Charade features Audrey Hepburn as a simultaneous interpreter in Paris, and The Interpreter stars Nicole Kidman as a United Nations interpreter. Both treat the profession as a backdrop to a thriller.

Is Lost in Translation really about translation?

Partly. The film is mostly about two people feeling isolated in Tokyo, but its title and one famous scene about interpreting made it a favourite among linguists. The scene shows how much meaning can be lost when an instruction is shortened.

Are there good French films about language and dialects?

Welcome to the Sticks is a popular French comedy that is built around the Ch'ti dialect of northern France. It is widely available with English subtitles, so you can see how the jokes are carried into another language.

Who translates film subtitles?

Professional subtitlers and dubbing teams adapt dialogue, humour and cultural references for a new audience, which goes well beyond word-for-word translation. The Okja subtitle joke is a good example of a deliberate adaptation.
